 More Than 25,000 Nursing Pillows Recalled
 Pillani nursing pillows don’t meet the mandatory safety standards for nursing pillows and can pose a risk of suffocation. No injuries have been reported. 
 By 
 Jessica D’Argenio Waller, MS, CNS, LDN, CPST 
 Baby & Health Writer 
 October 30, 2026 
 Source: CPSC
 Thousands of nursing pillows from the brand Pillani have been recalled for posing a risk of suffocation. The Consumer Product Safety Commission has issued a recall of U-shaped pillows for failing to meet mandatory safety standards for nursing pillows, which specify the shape, firmness, and design of the pillows. 
 No injuries or incidents have been reported regarding the recalled pillows, but because they violate the safety standard and can obstruct an infant’s breathing, consumers “should stop using the nursing pillows immediately and contact Pillani for a full refund,” the CPSC states. 
 The nursing pillows were sold on Amazon from April through September 2026 for about $30 to $40, and come in various prints and colorways. They have a U-shaped design with a narrow opening and a cloud-shaped pillow attached to provide back support for an infant, along with an adjustable waist strap for the feeding parent. The brand name, model number NP4351, and batch number 202604, 202605, or 202606 are printed on an attached label.
 What to Know About Nursing Pillow Safety
 Nursing pillows may seem like a low-risk baby product, but when nursing pillows are not used as intended, they can present a serious hazard —especially if used as a baby lounger or for infant sleep. Between 2010 and 2022, 154 infant deaths were associated with nursing pillows, along with 64 infant injuries, according to the CPSC . Most of the babies were under 3 months old, and they died from suffocation, entrapment, or falls associated with nursing pillows.
 Mandatory safety standards for nursing pillows were strengthened in 2025 to make the products safer and discourage their use as a sleeping space for babies. 
 Nursing Pillow Design Safety Changes
 To help prevent deaths and injuries from nursing pillows, the CPSC changed product regulations in four key ways:
 Clear warning labels advise on the hazards of misuse and urge parents not to use the pillow for infant sleep or to prop up a baby. 
 New firmness standards require nursing pillows to be sufficiently firm to prevent accidental infant suffocation and flatter in design to prevent use as infant loungers. 
 Wider openings are now required, so the pillow is designed to fit around an adult’s waist rather than prop up an infant. 
 No straps for baby are allowed, to discourage using a nursing pillow as a place to leave a baby unattended—but straps to allow a better fit for the nursing parent are still okay. 
 Nursing Pillow Regulations Tighten. Is Yours Safe?
 Significant design changes aim to make nursing pillows safer. Here’s what parents should know now . 
 How to Use a Nursing Pillow Safely With Your Baby
 The CPSC shares the following recommendations for staying safe with your nursing pillow—including pillows that were made before the new regulations went into effect:
 Only use your nursing pillow while feeding the baby. 
 Never use it for infant sleeping or lounging. 
 Do not put a nursing pillow in your baby’s crib or bassinet. 
 Do not leave your baby unattended on a nursing pillow, especially on an elevated surface. 
 If you or the baby gets sleepy, transfer the baby to a safe sleep space like the crib. 
 How to Choose a Nursing Pillow and Use It Safely
 Expert tips on what to look for in a safe nursing pillow, plus see the nursing pillows CR recommends .  
 Pillani Nursing Pillow Recall Details
 Products recalled: 25,762 Pillani nursing pillows have been recalled for failing to meet mandatory safety requirements and for obstructing an infant’s breathing, posing a risk of suffocation.

 Affected model numbers: The recalled pillows have model number NP4351 and batch number 202604, 202605, or 202606 printed on an attached label.
 The problem: The pillows fail to meet the required safety standards for nursing pillows and should not be used with infants. 
 What to do next: Stop using the recalled nursing pillows immediately, the CPSC says. You can contact Pillani for a full refund after first sending a photo of the product and following the disposal instructions. Contact Pillani by email at pillanirecall@gmail.com, or online at https://pill-ani.com/pages/recall or https://pill-ani.com and click “Recall” at the top of the page for more information.
 Jessica D’Argenio Waller, MS, CNS, LDN, CPST
 Jessica D’Argenio Waller is a baby and health writer and editor at Consumer Reports, covering a range of topics, from strollers to infant formula to safe sleep practices. Before joining CR in 2025, she was editorial director at Motherly. Jessica is a licensed and board-certified nutritionist and a certified child passenger safety technician, a mom of two, and an avid runner and home cook.
